entries.section: 1. Introduction:

paragraphs.text: The word of the LORD which came unto Zephaniah the son of Cushi, the son of Gedaliah, the son of Amariah, the son of Hizkiah, in the days of Josiah the son of Amon, king of Judah. [1]
The introduction to the book confirms that what the prophet Zephaniah records is not his own words, but the word of the Lord, declared to him from heaven.
He gives us the family tree back four generations, ending with King Hezekiah, who is mentioned in Second Kings (2 Kgs 18:1).

Josiah began the movement of reform in the twelfth year of his reign; so if the prophet Zephaniah began his prophecy at the beginning of Josiah's reign, then he certainly had his principal part in the movement of reform.

We should not wonder at the prophet's insistence on mentioning Amon, the idol worshiper, from whose offspring came Josiah, who did all that was in his power for religious and spiritual reform. On the one hand he wished to confirm the gravity of evil. For with all the effort that Josiah made, the people were as in an incurable sickness, since corruption had grown rampant among them because of Amon. On the other hand he wished to open before us the door of hope, for if the father was corrupt, as one from whom no good is expected, the young son defied the corruption of his father and set out to work in the spirit of power. And as the Lord Himself declares through Ezekiel the responsibility of every man for his own conduct, not for the deserts of his father: "Behold, all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine: the soul that sinneth, it shall die" (Ezek 18:4). "Now, lo, if he beget a son, that seeth all his father's sins, which he hath done, and considereth, and doeth not such like... he shall not die for the iniquity of his father, he shall surely live" (Ezek 18:14, 17).
* The soul that does not dwell in God is the source of its own evils, so it sins, and the soul that sins itself dies.
St. Ambrose

entries.section: 2. The desolation of Judah:

paragraphs.text: 2 "I will utterly consume all things from off the land, saith the LORD. 3 I will consume man and beast; I will consume the fowls of the heaven, and the fishes of the sea, and the stumblingblocks with the wicked; and I will cut off man from off the land, saith the LORD. 4 I will also stretch out mine hand upon Judah, and upon all the inhabitants of Jerusalem; and I will cut off the remnant of Baal from this place, and the name of the Chemarims with the priests; 5 And them that worship the host of heaven upon the housetops; and them that worship and that swear by the LORD, and that swear by Malcham; 6 And them that are turned back from the LORD; and those that have not sought the LORD, nor enquired for him."
I will utterly consume all things from off the land, saith the LORD. [2]

God created the earth that man might enjoy it as His ambassador and steward of heaven, so that the earth might be the icon of heaven; but now that man has become corrupt, God removes this earth from existence. For sin has corrupted man as it has corrupted the earth on which he lives. Moreover, the heavenly Word of God came down to our earth, to raise up from our hearts a second heaven, made fit by His grace for His dwelling. So he who insists on remaining earth and dust does not deserve to remain, but hears the divine voice: "I will utterly consume all things from off the land" [1]. But if we become heaven, we live with the Apostle Paul in the heavenly places; we are not removed, but enjoy the divine embraces eternally.

Thus as long as man insists on remaining earthy (of the earth), he drinks the golden cup of the bitterness of sin, so he becomes drunk and loses his balance, indeed his whole life. Therefore it is fitting for us to ask God to remove from our hearts everything that is earthly.

* "Babylon hath been a golden cup in the LORD'S hand, that made all the earth drunken" (Jer 28:7)... If you wish to know how all the earth has become drunken by the cup of Babylon, look at the sinners who fill the whole earth. But you may say to me that the righteous have not become drunken from the cup of sinners, so how does Scripture say that all the earth is made drunken from the cup of Babylon? Do not think that Scripture does not speak the truth when it says this, for the righteous in fact are not earth (dust), and therefore only all the earth, that is, the sinners alone, are those who become drunken. As for the righteous, although they are on the earth, their dwelling is in the heavens (Phil 3:20). Therefore it is not fitting that the righteous man should be told: "Thou art earth (dust), and unto earth (dust) shalt thou return," but the Lord will say to him, as long as that man wears the image of the heavenly (1 Cor 15:49): "Thou art heaven, and unto heaven shalt thou return." Therefore the cup of Babylon will not make drunken any but those who are still earth.
Origen I will consume man and beast.

entries.section: 2. The desolation of Judah:

paragraphs.text: I will consume the fowls of the heaven, and the fishes of the sea, and the stumblingblocks with the wicked; and I will cut off man from off the land, saith the LORD. [3]

He removes man and beast, either by captivity or by plagues that destroy them; and the air is corrupted until the fowls of the heaven die, and the waters are also corrupted so that the fishes of the sea die.

The Lord depicts the complete desolation that befalls mankind who deny their Creator, for He removes man and beast. If man signifies the rational human soul and the beast the animal body, then sin destroys the life of man as a whole: it deprives him of his rational nature, and it shatters his body as he thinks his happiness is in bodily pleasures.

He removes the fowls of the heaven and the fishes of the sea, for if man thinks that he is able to fly as though to heaven, or descend as though to the depths of the sea with the fishes, he will not be able to hide from the eye of God, nor to flee from the divine chastening, as the psalmist says: "Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy presence? If I ascend up into heaven, thou art there: if I make my bed in hell, behold, thou art there..." (Ps 139:7-8). It is fitting for him to flee not from God but to God Himself.
* Where shall the slave of sin flee? For he carries (his mistress, that is, sin) wherever he flees.
The evil conscience does not flee from itself; there is no place for it to go to.

Indeed it cannot withdraw from itself, for the sin it commits is within it. It commits sin in order to obtain some bodily pleasure. But the pleasure passes and the sin remains. What it delights in passes, and the thorn remains behind it. What an evil slavery...!
Let us all flee to Christ, and protest against sin to God as our Savior.

* He seeks a place to which he may flee from the wrath of God. What place protects the one who flees from God...? What place is there in which God is not? Who can deceive God? Who is there that God does not see?

* Let us flee in hope and longing on the wings of the double love (the love of God and the love of neighbor), so that we find no rest except in the depths of the sea (of love)... Let us flee to God in hope, and in a hope filled with faith let us contemplate at the end of the sea.

entries.section: 2. The desolation of Judah:

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine I will also stretch out mine hand upon Judah, and upon all the inhabitants of Jerusalem; and I will cut off the remnant of Baal from this place, and the name of the Chemarims with the priests. [4]

Since some thought that God would not permit the desolation of Judah because of the presence of the city of God, Jerusalem, and the Temple, the holy God declares that what concerns Him is neither Jerusalem nor the Temple as a building, but holiness, which He desires for all mankind; if men lose the holy life, He is ready to remove the whole earth with all that is on it, which He created for the sake of man.

If God stretches out His hand to chasten Judah in general, He chastens all the more Jerusalem, which was consecrated as the city of God containing the holy Temple, because she permitted the mixing of the worship of God with pagan worship. He declared that He will cut off the name of Baal and his worship from the land, and the Chemarims [priests of the idols (2 Kgs 23:5)] who were leading the people astray. He cuts them off with their idols, and also cuts off those who worship the stars, and those who swear by the name of Malcham.
"Baal" is the Phoenician guardian god. Israel fell into this pagan worship from the time of the judges (Judg 2:13). King Manasseh set up an image of Baal in the Temple itself (2 Kgs 21:3, 5, 7).

Chemarim: the Hebrew origin is derived from a word whose meaning is "black," since the priests wore black garments and also placed a black mark on their foreheads. Some think that the priests of Molech were called the black men because of the continual smoke that rose from the altar on which they burned human sacrifices, where some offered their children as sacrifices. So the faces of the priests were black. The word chemarim also means "jealousy," because of their fanaticism and their zeal for spreading paganism.

entries.section: 2. The desolation of Judah:

paragraphs.text: And them that worship the host of heaven upon the housetops; and them that worship and that swear by the LORD, and that swear by Malcham. [5]

God rejects the mixing of what belongs to God with what belongs to the devil, and the fellowship between light and darkness. For when a part of the heart is surrendered to the devil, he storms it to reign over it completely, and if a part of the heart is left to God, He rejects it completely and departs from it. The devil by his deceit creeps in to reign completely, and God in His love will not force Himself in unless the heart is completely surrendered to Him that He may set up His Kingdom in it.
Some were accustomed to mixing the worship of the living God with the worship of idols, and to adding to their oath by the living God the name or names of pagan gods.
The worship of the sun or the moon or one of the stars was a common thing, and is among the oldest of pagan worships.

entries.section: 2. The desolation of Judah:

paragraphs.text: And them that are turned back from the LORD; and those that have not sought the LORD, nor enquired for him. [6]

Here he divides the people into two groups: one group responded to the call of King Josiah to repentance, but only for a time, then turned back from the LORD to practice pagan abominations. These put their hands to the plough and looked back. As for the second group, they did not respond to the call of the king, and the Lord did not concern them at all.

The book concentrates on three main errors, which are: 1. The worship of idols [4-5]. 2. Halting between the two parties, at one time swearing by the living God and at another by Malcham [5]. 3. Turning the back to God [6].

entries.section: 3. The day of the Lord is near:

paragraphs.text: 7 "Hold thy peace at the presence of the Lord GOD: for the day of the LORD is at hand: for the LORD hath prepared a sacrifice, he hath bid his guests. 8 And it shall come to pass in the day of the LORD'S sacrifice, that I will punish the princes, and the king's children, and all such as are clothed with strange apparel. 9 In the same day also will I punish all those that leap on the threshold, which fill their masters' houses with violence and deceit. 10 And it shall come to pass in that day, saith the LORD, that there shall be the noise of a cry from the fish gate, and an howling from the second, and a great crashing from the hills. 11 Howl, ye inhabitants of Maktesh, for all the people of Canaan are cut down; all they that bear silver are cut off. 12 And it shall come to pass at that time, that I will search Jerusalem with candles, and punish the men that are settled on their lees: that say in their heart, The LORD will not do good, neither will he do evil. 13 Therefore their goods shall become a booty, and their houses a desolation: they shall also build houses, but not inhabit them; and they shall plant vineyards, but not drink the wine thereof."
Hold thy peace at the presence of the Lord GOD: for the day of the LORD is at hand.
For the LORD hath prepared a sacrifice.
He hath bid his guests. [7]

Since many mocked the words of the prophets that threatened the destruction of Jerusalem, saying that generation after generation had passed and nothing of this had happened, and that the prophets were threatening what would never be fulfilled, the prophet Zephaniah says: "The day of the LORD is at hand" [7].

The present time is regarded as the days of men, who do as they please, but the last day, when God proclaims His eternal Kingdom and gathers to Himself His true believers, is the day of the Lord, and every man is judged according to his works. The weekly day of worship is also regarded as the day of the Lord, when the believer consecrates this day to worship that it may be a mystery of blessing for the whole week. Also the day of chastening that is accomplished in this age, at the time appropriate for each one, is counted as the day of the Lord, and it is near.

He permitted the Babylonians to kill and slaughter the Jews when they triumphed over Judah, and these slain were counted as though they were a sacrifice offered by the priests to the Lord. Here the prophet depicts their slaughter in bitterness: they are killed without mercy and without stirring of conscience, but their killers count them a sacrifice offered to the Lord! They exult and rejoice while killing them by offering human sacrifices as on a day of feast.

The word of the Lord came describing that day: "For this is the day of the Lord GOD of hosts, a day of vengeance, that he may avenge him of his adversaries: and the sword shall devour, and it shall be satiate and made drunk with their blood: for the Lord GOD of hosts hath a sacrifice in the north country by the river Euphrates" (Jer 46:10). It was also said: "And thou, son of man, thus saith the Lord GOD; Speak unto every feathered fowl, and to every beast of the field, Assemble yourselves, and come; gather yourselves on every side to my sacrifice that I do sacrifice for you, even a great sacrifice upon the mountains of Israel, that ye may eat flesh, and drink blood. Ye shall eat the flesh of the mighty, and drink the blood of the princes of the earth" (Ezek 39:17-18).

entries.section: 3. The day of the Lord is near:

paragraphs.text: And it shall come to pass in the day of the LORD'S sacrifice, that I will punish the princes, and the king's children, and all such as are clothed with strange apparel. [8]
When the Lord chastens His people He begins with the princes and the king's children and the nobles, and the leaders like them, as with the rest of the sinning classes, without partiality.

Since God permitted Nebuchadnezzar to slaughter the wicked great men of Judah, offering them as a sacrifice, he began with the princes or the rulers, for they ought to have been an example to the people, but they became a stumblingblock to them. This prophecy was fulfilled when the sons of Zedekiah were killed (Jer 39:6).

"All such as are clothed with strange apparel" means the princes and the men of the court who wore garments imported from abroad, very costly, as a kind of luxury and grandeur; and perhaps these garments belonged to the pagans, who made a show of them during pagan worship. By wearing these garments they were counted as having shared in pagan worship. Some think that the strange garments are those that the Law forbade, such as men wearing women's garments, and the reverse also (Deut 22:5).

entries.section: 3. The day of the Lord is near:

paragraphs.text: In the same day also will I punish all those that leap on the threshold, which fill their masters' houses with violence and deceit. [9]

"Those that leap on the threshold": an expression that usually means a man's assault on the rights of his neighbor, like one who leaps over the threshold to seize something from his neighbor's house by violence as well as by deceit.

Some think that it means here those who flatter the royal court, where they were seizing what belonged to others for their masters, so they are like hunting dogs that leap over the threshold to seize the property of others for the men of the palace. Others see in it a reference to the Philistines, who seized the ark of God and brought it to Ashdod, and entered with it into the house of Dagon and set it beside the god Dagon; and when the latter fell on his face to the ground before the ark of the covenant, with his head and his hands cut off on the threshold, the priests and all who entered used to leap so as not to tread on the threshold with their feet, and this became a custom for all who enter the temple of Dagon (1 Sam 5:1-5). St. Jerome sees that it refers here to those who go up the steps of the Temple in haughtiness and pride.

entries.section: 3. The day of the Lord is near:

paragraphs.text: And it shall come to pass in that day, saith the LORD, that there shall be the noise of a cry from the fish gate, and an howling from the second, and a great crashing from the hills. [10]

The fish gate: this gate is mentioned in Nehemiah (Neh 3:3); it is opposite Joppa, and perhaps it is the gate from which came the news of the violent storming of the Chaldean army from the region of the hills. It was called the fish gate because of its nearness to the fish market, and because the fishermen coming from the Lake of Tiberias and the River Jordan used to pass through this gate.
When the cry arose from the fish gate, the reaction was in the second quarter or the lower part of the city, where they howled on hearing the cries that were coming.
When the cries resounded around the walls of Jerusalem, coming from the surrounding mountains, resounding from gate to gate, surely despair befell all the inhabitants in the safest regions.
Howl, ye inhabitants of Maktesh, for all the people of Canaan are cut down.

entries.section: 3. The day of the Lord is near:

paragraphs.text: All they that bear silver are cut off. [11]

Evil was found in Maktesh, in a low and deep place in the city, like a mortar. The merchants and businessmen dwelt there at ease, but desolation befell them, and there was no longer any bearer of silver or money entering for trade! Its people became ground, as wheat or medicine is ground in a mortar. In the Book of Ezekiel He likens it to the pot into which every good piece is put: the thigh and the shoulder with the choice bones, and He boils it until its bones are also seethed in the midst of it (Ezek 24:3-5).
Some think that it refers here not to a particular location in Jerusalem but to the whole city, where the people are struck and crushed to death like wheat in the mortar.

Maktesh or Mortar, that is, a mortar; it is a name that applies to the valley of Siloam by its hollow shape. This valley is between Zion and Mount Olivet at the extreme eastern side of Mount Moriah, where the merchants dwell. Perhaps it was near the fish gate.
And it shall come to pass at that time, that I will search Jerusalem with candles, and punish the men that are settled on their lees: that say in their heart,

entries.section: 3. The day of the Lord is near:

paragraphs.text: The LORD will not do good, neither will he do evil. [12]

When some see the righteous in distress while the wicked enjoy success and prosperity, they often ask: Where is divine justice? Where is the reward that the righteous receive? And where is the punishment that befalls the wicked? Where is God's care and concern for mankind?

Here God, as He chastens Jerusalem for her evils, is pictured holding candles, searching even in the hidden, dark places, that no wicked man may escape the divine chastening. Here the Lord searches Jerusalem with candles not to look for the lost piece of silver (Lk 15:8-10), for He has given the sinners many opportunities to return to Him; therefore He uses the candles to single out the wicked who insist on despising God's warnings, in order to chasten them.

God punishes not only those who become drunk with the wine of the love of luxury and the world, but even those who drink what remains of the sediment in the wine bottles (the dregs). These in their drunkenness fall into practical atheism, where they do not deny the existence of God, but deny His providence over the world or His concern for mankind, as though man does not concern Him at all.

In this chapter the Lord appears as one who is in the midst of Judah to judge her or chasten her, but in the last chapter He announces His dwelling in the midst of mankind that she may rejoice in Him as He delights in her, for she is the place of His pleasure. Here He announces His chastening of Judah, which worships idols, a thing that God cannot bear in His people.

* The Lord Jesus came to Jerusalem, into the Temple. And when he had looked round about upon all things, and now the eventide was come, he went out unto Bethany with the twelve (Mk 11:11). The Lord entered Jerusalem, into the Temple. And when He entered, what did He do? He looked round about upon all things. He was in the temple of the Jews seeking a place to lay His head, and found none...
He looked at the Jews; and He wished to be in their midst, but He did not find them...
He was assessing everything around Him like one searching with a candle, therefore the prophet Zephaniah says: "I will search Jerusalem with candles" (Zeph 1:12).

In the same way the Lord also looked around Him upon all things by the light of a candle. He was searching in the Temple and did not find what He sought, until evening came and He was still examining everything... As long as there was light, He remained in the Temple. But when evening had come, when the shadows of ignorance had fallen, so the temple of the Jews became dark, He went out to Bethany with the twelve.
The Savior searched, and the Apostles searched, and when they found nothing in the Temple they left it.

St. Jerome * This question is often repeated in the minds of those who do not have great faith and knowledge, thinking that the reward of the saints, which is not given in this world but in the life to come, is granted to them in this short period of transient life. But we have set our hope in Christ, not in this life, lest we become, as the Apostle says, of all men most miserable (1 Cor 15:19).
For God does not keep trials away from the upright, nor does He reward in this world the righteous with profitable things and the wicked with evil things.

If we say otherwise, we fall into punishment with those whom the prophet Zephaniah mentions: "that say in their heart, The LORD will not do good, neither will he do evil" (Zeph 1:12). Or at the least we become among the blasphemers against God who say: "Every one that doeth evil is good in the sight of the LORD, and he delighteth in them; or, Where is the God of judgment?" (Mal 2:17), and we fall into the blasphemy that he (the prophet) described thus: "Ye have said, It is vain to serve God: and what profit is it that we have kept his ordinance, and that we have walked mournfully before the LORD of hosts? And now we call the proud happy; yea, they that work wickedness are set up; yea, they that tempt God are even delivered" (Mal 3:14-15).

entries.section: 3. The day of the Lord is near:

paragraphs.text: Father Theodore Therefore their goods shall become a booty, and their houses a desolation: they shall also build houses, but not inhabit them; and they shall plant vineyards, but not drink the wine thereof. [13]

Although God in His long-suffering does not hasten to impose punishment on the wicked, waiting for their repentance through His tenderness toward them, yet surely if they do not return they will drink from the cup that they have filled.

The enemy strips them of everything, of their wealth, and of their houses that are the work of their hands, as well as of their vineyards that they planted, for the invaders seize everything. Thus the prophecy recorded in (Deut 28:30, 39) is fulfilled concerning the one who does not hearken to the voice of the Lord: "Thou shalt betroth a wife, and another man shall lie with her: thou shalt build an house, and thou shalt not dwell therein: thou shalt plant a vineyard, and shalt not gather the grapes thereof... Thou shalt plant vineyards, and dress them, but shalt neither drink of the wine, nor gather the grapes; for the worms shall eat them."

St. Jerome uses this phrase with other passages of Holy Scripture to make clear that there is nothing in this world that can satisfy the depths of man. He says: [We must not seek the lust of possessions and money; it is written in Solomon, in the Book of Ecclesiastes: "He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver" (Eccl 5:10). And in Proverbs: "He that withholdeth corn, the people shall curse him: but blessing shall be upon the head of him that selleth it" (Prov 11:26). Also in Isaiah: "Woe unto them that join house to house, that lay field to field, till there be no place, that they may be placed alone in the midst of the earth!" (Isa 5:8). And also in Zephaniah: "They shall also build houses, but not inhabit them; and they shall plant vineyards, but not drink the wine thereof; for the day of the LORD is near" (Zeph 1:13-14). And in the Gospel according to Luke: "For what is a man advantaged, if he gain the whole world, and lose himself, or be cast away?" (Lk 9:25)].

* Concerning that day the prophet Amos says: "Woe unto you that desire the day of the LORD! to what end is it for you? the day of the LORD is darkness, and not light" (Amos 5:18). And the prophet Zephaniah says the same thing: "The voice of the day of the LORD is dreadful and bitter" (Zeph 1:14-15). This is the reason why the penitent person is presented to us seeking earnestly in his prayer that he may not be judged for his works on that day of judgment. What is more profitable and far-sighted for a person than to pray for the fatherly love of God while he is still in this world, where there is opportunity for repentance, he who cannot have hope in his deserts because of the sins he has committed?

Cassiodorus * There is a light that can be perceived by the senses, of which it was said in Moses that it came into being on the fourth day, but it is not the true light, for it illumines the things that are on the earth. On the other hand, the Savior is the light of the spiritual world, for He shines upon the rational and the thinking, that their minds may see fitting visions. I mean that He is the light of the rational souls that are in the perceptible world, of whom the Savior teaches us that He is its Creator and its Director... He is the sun of the great day of the Lord.
Origen

entries.section: 4. The great day of the Lord:

paragraphs.text: 14 "The great day of the LORD is near, it is near, and hasteth greatly, even the voice of the day of the LORD: the mighty man shall cry there bitterly. 15 That day is a day of wrath, a day of trouble and distress, a day of wasteness and desolation, a day of darkness and gloominess, a day of clouds and thick darkness, 16 A day of the trumpet and alarm against the fenced cities, and against the high towers. 17 And I will bring distress upon men, that they shall walk like blind men, because they have sinned against the LORD: and their blood shall be poured out as dust, and their flesh as the dung. 18 Neither their silver nor their gold shall be able to deliver them in the day of the LORD'S wrath; but the whole land shall be devoured by the fire of his jealousy: for he shall make even a sudden riddance of all them that dwell in the land."
The great day of the LORD is near.
It is near, and hasteth greatly.
Even the voice of the day of the LORD.
The mighty man shall cry there bitterly. [14]

Here the prophet gives a warning to Judah and Jerusalem of the nearness of the destruction that will befall by the Babylonians. It is not the day of the Babylonians, but "the great day of the LORD is near," for this destruction is only by the permission of the Lord to chasten them.

The prophet affirms that the day of chastening has become near and very swift; there is no time for slackness or postponement. Here, while he prophesies of the day of the captivity of Judah as the great day of the Lord, he also prophesies of the great day of judgment, when all mankind stand before the Lord.

These are very brief and repeated cries, for the danger is extremely grave and the time very short; there is no room for dialogue. It is like a man who sees his family inside the house and the fire beginning to blaze in it, so he cries out that perhaps all will hasten to go out by the nearest door or leap from the nearest window. And as was said by the prophet Amos: "The LORD will roar from Zion, and utter his voice from Jerusalem; and the habitations of the shepherds shall mourn, and the top of Carmel shall wither" (Amos 1:2).

This day began with the death of the good king Josiah, whom Pharaoh Necho killed at the battle of Megiddo, and the day continued until the destruction of Jerusalem was accomplished at the hand of Nebuchadnezzar the Babylonian.

The world's gold and silver cannot deliver us on the great day of the Lord, but the believer's wealth is the divine commandment; whoever keeps it, it keeps him from the divine wrath. The commandment is a treasure, which we acquire by the work of divine grace, so we bear the righteousness of Christ.
That day is a day of wrath, a day of trouble and distress.
A day of wasteness and desolation.
A day of darkness and gloominess.

entries.section: 4. The great day of the Lord:

paragraphs.text: A day of clouds and thick darkness. [15]

The great day of the Lord is a day of joyful wedding for the believers who have prepared for the wedding through the riches of God's surpassing grace, and a day of wrath, distress, wasteness, desolation, darkness and gloominess for those who have not prepared for it by living faith working through love.

Human languages are no longer able to express the extent of the desolation that befalls Judah, so the prophet offers many synonyms that perhaps may depict the gravity of that day, so he calls it a day of wrath, as also a day of trouble and distress, of wasteness and desolation, of darkness and gloominess, of trumpet and alarm, and so on.

A grave picture, where the whirlwinds of divine wrath blow, so distress comes with total desolation, and all become like people in darkness, with no one having insight to see a way of salvation, and no one able to offer useful counsel. It is a day of dense cloud and fog that no man can resist or face.

entries.section: 4. The great day of the Lord:

paragraphs.text: A day of the trumpet and alarm against the fenced cities, and against the high towers. [16]

What citadel or fortress or walls can stand in the face of God's wrath? Those who think they are hidden in fortified cities and high towers hear the sounds of the trumpets of war and the shouts of the hostile armies, so their whole being collapses and their strength dissolves!

entries.section: 4. The great day of the Lord:

paragraphs.text: And I will bring distress upon men, that they shall walk like blind men, because they have sinned against the LORD: and their blood shall be poured out as dust, and their flesh as the dung. [17]

The wicked on the great day of the Lord will be like the blind, for they are unable to enjoy the splendor of God's glory; they see God as a mighty Judge, not as a heavenly Bridegroom who gives His people fellowship in glory with Him.

Those who walk in evil, and resist the truth, and do not hearken to the voice of the Lord and His commandment are like blind men groping here and there, always in doubt and in danger! They search for a way of escape, but because of the blindness of their insight they do not see an escape that would save them.

Everything they touch and are certain of is that the sword strikes among them and their blood bursts forth, and their bodies fall under the feet of the enemy, with no one to bind up a wound and no one to lift a corpse from the dust!

entries.section: 4. The great day of the Lord:

paragraphs.text: Neither their silver nor their gold shall be able to deliver them in the day of the LORD'S wrath; but the whole land shall be devoured by the fire of his jealousy: for he shall make even a sudden riddance of all them that dwell in the land. [18]

As they kindle the fire of divine jealousy by their disobedience and their abominations and their resistance to God, destruction befalls all, and the blow strikes the whole earth, so there is no hidden place in it to which anyone may flee. Here all the wealth they acquired unjustly cannot protect them from destruction. And as the wise man says: "Riches profit not in the day of wrath: but righteousness delivereth from death" (Prov 11:4).

* I am anxious and troubled as I speak of the multitude of ornaments; and I am obliged to be astonished how those who bear such a weight are not troubled by death. What a toil full of folly! What an absurd madness is exposed...! The rich man, as he fills his barns, says to his soul: "Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry." And behold, the Lord in the Gospels plainly calls him: "Thou fool" (Lk 12:20), "this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?" When the painter Apelles saw one of his pupils painting a picture of a person laden with a golden color to present it to Helen, he said to him: "Boy, since you are unable to paint her beautiful, you have painted her rich." Concerning these the prophet Zephaniah says: "Neither their silver nor their gold shall be able to deliver them in the day of the LORD'S wrath" (Zeph 1:18). For it is fitting for these women who are being trained under the hands of Christ not to adorn themselves with gold but with the Word, through whom alone gold appears in the light.

St. Clement of Alexandria * Let us show the perfection of the obedience that is inspired in us by the expectation of His coming. Let us not hasten as slaves hasten, and defend ourselves before the Lord in a shameful and disgraceful manner. Rather let us persevere and strive and watch with all our hearts, and stand firm to the end. Let us keep the commandments of the Lord so that when the day of wrath and vengeance comes we may not be punished with the sinners and the wicked, but may be honored with the righteous and those who fear the Lord.
The martyr Cyprian
May Your great day come!
* My soul often asks:
When will Your great day come?
Truly, the wicked man thinks that all the days are his day, so he acts arrogantly, and the righteous man groans, awaiting the day of Your great coming.
When will You come and support every soul in the midst of its groaning?
* You promised that You are coming quickly to chasten.
Chasten me in Your mercy, before Your coming on the clouds.
For I cannot flee from You, but I flee to You.
You are my refuge; I take shelter in You, so that wrath may not befall me!
If I ascend into heaven, You are there; and if I go down to Hades, I find You before me.
I flee to You, O Heavenly One.
Remove from me everything earthly by Your fiery Spirit.
So I shall become a second heaven for You, which destruction will not approach!
* May Your great day come now, for I know that You destroy in me everything that is evil, and cover me with Your righteousness and holiness!
* I await the coming of Your great last day!
I see You as the radiant Bridegroom, not the fearful Judge!
I see Your eyes as doves, but the wicked see them as burning fire.
The day of Your coming is a day of light and splendor, not a day of darkness and gloominess.
Your coming is the constant desire of my heart, and not a day of trouble and distress, wasteness and desolation.
Come on the clouds, and take me with You, that I may enter with You into the bosom of the Father!

entries.section: 1. A call to his people to seek righteousness:

paragraphs.text: 1 Gather yourselves together, yea, gather together, O nation not desired; 2 Before the decree bring forth, before the day pass as the chaff, before the fierce anger of the LORD come upon you, before the day of the LORD’s anger come upon you. 3 Seek ye the LORD, all ye meek of the earth, which have wrought his judgment; seek righteousness, seek meekness: it may be ye shall be hid in the day of the LORD’s anger.

Before He begins to judge the nations that gloat over His people who are under discipline, He asks His people to repent and to seek righteousness and humility, so that the Lord may cover them and restore their glory to them. He does not judge those who gloat over His people unless the latter offer sincere repentance.
Gather yourselves together, yea, gather together, O nation not desired. [1]

He calls this nation, which considered itself God’s people, distinguished from the rest of the nations and peoples, to review its position, for it is a “nation not desired,” or “a nation not desiring God,” or one that has nothing to commend it before Him. He asks it to gather itself and to gather together, for one of the grave fruits of sin is the loss of the common purpose, so that each one acts according to his own whim. As it was said of the dark period of the Judges: “In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes” (Judg 21:25).
Sin makes a person like chaff that has no place of rest, and turns society into a storm that scatters and disperses everyone.

On the contrary, the work of true repentance is the return of a person to his depths, to look by the Spirit of truth into his heart, his thought, his feelings, his intentions and his will… Here he cleaves to God, and so draws near to his brethren in the spirit of unity, not by mere bodily gathering, but so that all have one Spirit and one mind.

Here the call to gather with her is perhaps so that all may review their accounts together, offer a communal repentance, and turn away from themselves the shame and the divine wrath, in a spirit of prayer, reverence and desire to return to Him.
Before the decree bring forth.
Before the day pass as the chaff.
Before the fierce anger of the LORD come upon you.

entries.section: 1. A call to his people to seek righteousness:

paragraphs.text: Before the day of the LORD’s anger come upon you. [2]
If His people have fallen under discipline, He warns them that unless they return to Him they will fall under the divine wrath in the day of the LORD’s anger.

If sin corrupts people’s lives and makes of them straw rather than wheat, then the slightest attack of an enemy becomes like the wind, and the straw is scattered and dispersed. But repentance makes wheat of the straw, so that the winds do not scatter them, but rather cleanse them of the straw so that the wheat is gathered together.
He asks them for swift and zealous repentance, for the day of the birth of the decree, or the day of divine discipline, has drawn very near; it is at the doors.

Perhaps He likens the day of the Lord here to chaff, which comes swiftly when the winds of divine wrath blow; and when the day comes the wicked find no opportunity to flee, for it will pass like chaff that is hard to overtake, and they themselves become chaff in the blast of violent winds! As the psalmist says: “The ungodly are not so: but are like the chaff which the wind driveth away” (Ps 1:4). And as the Lord says of the wicked people of Ephraim: “Therefore they shall be as the morning cloud, and as the early dew that passeth away, as the chaff that is driven with the whirlwind out of the floor, and as the smoke out of the chimney” (Hos 13:3).
Thus the wicked find no place of rest; they do not settle upon the earth, nor do they reach heaven. They are like the storm that the wind drives in every direction.

St. Augustine compares the meek with the wicked. Of the meek it was said: “Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth” (Mt 5:5); but the wicked are like dust (and ashes) that the wind drives away from the face of the earth (Ps 1:4). For pride puffs up the wicked man, so that he is always driven away from the face of the earth.

* The wicked are “like the chaff which the wind driveth away” (Ps 1:4). Scripture says that the wicked man is unhappy, so that he is not even like the dust of the earth. Dust appears as though it had no being, yet it has a kind of existence in itself… It is scattered here and there and has no place in which to settle; wherever the wind sweeps it, its strength is dissipated. So is the wicked man: since he denies God, he is led by error, wherever the breezes of the devil send him.

St. Jerome * “Let them be as chaff before the wind: and let the angel of the LORD chase them” (Ps 35:5)… The wind is temptation, and the dust (the chaff) is the wicked. When temptation comes the dust rises and does not stand before the wind nor resist it.
St. Augustine Seek ye the LORD, all ye meek of the earth, which have wrought his judgment;
Seek righteousness,
Seek meekness.

entries.section: 1. A call to his people to seek righteousness:

paragraphs.text: It may be ye shall be hid in the day of the LORD’s anger. [3]

In calling them to gather together He did not wish each of them to instill in the other a spirit of terror and dread, but that they gather together to seek the Lord. They seek the Lord that He may pour out His grace upon them and have mercy on them, and fulfill His promises to them. He calls them to gather in a spirit of gentleness, like sick people asking the heavenly Physician to stretch out His hand to treat and heal. Therefore He calls them: “all ye wretched (meek) of the earth.”

It is remarkable that He calls the meek of the earth (the wretched of the earth) to seek the Lord Himself and to ask Him for righteousness and humility; by this they are hidden in the day of the LORD’s anger. There is no way to hide from wrath except by taking refuge in the Lord and hiding in Him, and enjoying the divine righteousness, which covers their weaknesses, and obtaining humility, so that they become wheat instead of being chaff in the blast of the raging wind.

The Lord proclaimed this same call in the book of Isaiah: “Come, my people, enter thou into thy chambers, and shut thy doors about thee: hide thyself as it were for a little moment, until the indignation be overpast. For, behold, the LORD cometh out of his place to punish the inhabitants of the earth for their iniquity” (Isa 26:20-21). And in Amos: “For thus saith the LORD unto the house of Israel, Seek ye me, and ye shall live… Seek the LORD, and ye shall live; lest he break out like fire in the house of Joseph, and devour it, and there be none to quench it in Beth-el” (Amos 5:4, 6).

Some see that the address here is directed to the class of the wretched who fell under oppression because of the corruption that had come upon the land, and the exploitation of the opportunity against the poor by the powerful and the rich. Yet these poor also shared in the corruption and the abominations; therefore the prophet asks them to return to the Lord and seek His mercy by repentance in humility and by walking in righteousness. For the oppression that has come upon them will not justify them on the day of the LORD’s anger unless they return to Him with all their hearts.

Perhaps he means by the wretched here the Jews who crucified Christ; if they blasphemed Him and crucified Him, let them recognize Him and seek Him in a spirit of humility, and He will embrace them and keep them from the wrath that came upon them because of their denial of Him. For it was said to them by the prophet Isaiah: “Seek ye the LORD while he may be found, call ye upon him while he is near” (Isa 55:6).

St. Cyprian sees in the call “Seek the Lord” an invitation to leave everything in order to seek the Lord and His Kingdom and His righteousness, and then everything will be added to us, as the Lord Christ Himself said (Mt 6:31-33).

* While there is time, look to true and eternal salvation, and since the end of the world is at the doors, turn your minds in the fear of the Lord to God. Do not rejoice in your vain authority, which without power rules in this world over the righteous and the meek… “Seek the LORD, and ye shall live” (Amos 5:6). Know the Lord, even if the time is late… Believe in Him, who will not deceive you. Believe in Him who foretold to you the coming of all these things. Believe in Him who will give eternal life to those who believe. Believe in Him who by the fires of hell will inflict eternal punishment on those who do not believe.
The martyr Cyprian Thus we have no refuge from the wrath of the Lord except fleeing to Him and taking shelter in Him.
* Before we sought the Lord we were weak and unstable; now that our hearts are settled upon Him we are strong and courageous.
St. Jerome

entries.section: 2. The judgment of Philistia:

paragraphs.text: 4 For Gaza shall be forsaken, and Ashkelon a desolation: they shall drive out Ashdod at the noon day, and Ekron shall be rooted up. 5 Woe unto the inhabitants of the sea coast, the nation of the Cherethites! the word of the LORD is against you; O Canaan, the land of the Philistines, I will even destroy thee, that there shall be no inhabitant. 6 And the sea coast shall be dwellings and cottages for shepherds, and folds for flocks. 7 And the coast shall be for the remnant of the house of Judah; they shall feed thereupon: in the houses of Ashkelon shall they lie down in the evening: for the LORD their God shall visit them, and turn away their captivity.
For Gaza shall be forsaken, and Ashkelon a desolation.
They shall drive out Ashdod at the noon day, and Ekron shall be rooted up. [4]

The Lord disciplines the important cities of Philistia, which prided themselves in arrogance upon their power or prosperity, namely Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod and Ekron. The city of Gaza becomes forsaken, like a barren wilderness; Alexander the Great destroyed it completely, so that he almost erased it. Its name in Hebrew came as “deceitful, Gazubah,” which carries this meaning, that is, without existence. As for the second city, Ashkelon, in Hebrew it is Ekron teeaker.

Ashdod is driven out at the time of noon. The Easterners have known from ancient times that they sleep at noon because of the heat, so it is considered a time of idleness (2 Sam 4:5), and military operations used to stop during that period.

It is noted that the fifth well-known city of Philistia, “Gath,” is not mentioned here because at that time it was subject to the Jews. For this reason Zephaniah here, and Amos (Amos 1:6), Jeremiah (Jer 25:20) and Zechariah (Zech 9:5-6) mentioned only the four cities.

What he prophesies here concerning these four principal cities points to what befalls the wicked, unrepentant man, namely that he suffers isolation, being forsaken; desolation, where the divine righteousness does not dwell in him; terror, where he lives as a fugitive with none pursuing him; and finally being rooted up, where his life ends with the fate of the enemy of good himself.

This is the divine warning to every man who chooses for himself to resist the divine truth and to turn his back on God, the Giver of life, satisfaction, peace and happiness. He groans with Zion, who in her bitterness thought that the Lord had forsaken her and her Lord had forgotten her (Isa 49:14), and says: “Behold, I was left alone” (Isa 49:21). And as the prophet Jeremiah says: “Every city shall be forsaken, and not a man dwell therein” (Jer 4:29). As was said by the prophet Isaiah: “And they shall look unto the earth; and behold trouble and darkness, dimness of anguish; and they shall be driven to darkness” (Isa 8:22). And as was said by the psalmist: “Let their habitation be desolate; and let none dwell in their tents” (Ps 69:25); “How are they brought into desolation, as in a moment!” (Ps 73:19). And it is said in the Maccabees: “He rooted out every wicked and evil man” (1 Macc 14:14).

* “How are they brought into desolation, as in a moment!” (Ps 73:19) He marvels at them, perceiving what will finally befall them. “They have vanished”; truly they have become like smoke, which, as it ascends on high, vanishes; so have they vanished… “They are consumed by their iniquities.” They are like a dream when one awaketh (Ps 73:20)… When a man sees that he has found treasures while he sleeps, he is only under the illusion that he is rich, but until he awakes… he searches and does not find; there is nothing in his hands, nothing in his bed… These (the wicked), when they awake, find the misery that they prepared for themselves.

St. Augustine If evil demolishes a person and robs him of all vitality, so that he is like one abandoned in isolation, destruction comes upon him and he is rooted up, then God who permits this does so in order to root out the evil in him and to plant him anew, that is, to renew his life and nature by His Holy Spirit. He shatters the evil in us in order to establish His righteousness in us. As the psalmist says: “Thou with thy hand hast rooted out the nations, and planted them” (Ps 44:2).
Woe unto the inhabitants of the sea coast, the nation of the Cherethites.

entries.section: 2. The judgment of Philistia:

paragraphs.text: The word of the LORD is against you; O Canaan, the land of the Philistines, I will even destroy thee, that there shall be no inhabitant. [5]
By the sea coast is meant the whole region on the shore of the Mediterranean Sea from Egypt to Joppa and Gaza. The Hebrew word is Ceroth, which corresponds in sound to “water basins, dug cisterns.”

entries.section: 2. The judgment of Philistia:

paragraphs.text: And the sea coast shall be dwellings and cottages for shepherds, and folds for flocks. [6]

The sea coast, which was used as a harbor for ships and inhabited by merchants, becomes empty of inhabitants. It is transformed from a commercial land full of activity and vitality into a pasture for sheep and folds.

Some see that by the nation of the Cherethites is meant a group of sojourners or immigrants from Phoenicia, mentioned in (1 Sam 30:14; Amos 9:7). In the Septuagint and the Syriac it appears under the name “Crete.”
And the coast shall be for the remnant of the house of Judah.
They shall feed thereupon.

entries.section: 2. The judgment of Philistia:

paragraphs.text: In the houses of Ashkelon shall they lie down in the evening: for the LORD their God shall visit them, and turn away their captivity. [7]
He prophesies here that the house of Judah will regain its possession of Ashkelon, and that the remnant returning from captivity will settle in safety in the houses of Ashkelon.

Alexander the Great destroyed Ashkelon, and the Maccabees fulfilled what the prophets had prophesied against it, as it lost its system of government completely, and the people were finally compelled to be circumcised, that is, to enter Judaism by force.

entries.section: 3. The judgment of Moab and Ammon:

paragraphs.text: 8 I have heard the reproach of Moab, and the revilings of the children of Ammon, whereby they have reproached my people, and magnified themselves against their border. 9 Therefore as I live, saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, Surely Moab shall be as Sodom, and the children of Ammon as Gomorrah, even the breeding of nettles, and saltpits, and a perpetual desolation: the residue of my people shall spoil them, and the remnant of my people shall possess them. 10 This shall they have for their pride, because they have reproached and magnified themselves against the people of the LORD of hosts. 11 The LORD will be terrible unto them: for he will famish all the gods of the earth; and men shall worship him, every one from his place, even all the isles of the heathen.
I have heard the reproach of Moab, and the revilings of the children of Ammon, whereby they have reproached my people, and magnified themselves against their border. [8]

The sons of Moab and the sons of Ammon are linked together, for each of Moab and Ammon is an illegitimate son of the fallen Lot (Gen 19:33-38). These two peoples represent those who are bastards and not children of God, for they refuse to believe in the Lord Christ and do not enjoy the new spiritual birth.

The sons of Moab and the sons of Ammon fell under discipline because they mocked the Jewish people during their discipline and blasphemed their God. In their mockery and gloating over them they thought that the God of Israel did not hear and had no power to resist them; therefore He says: “I have heard the reproach of Moab and the revilings of the children of Ammon,” even though in His long-suffering He seemed as one who does not hear until He disciplines His people.
“Magnified themselves against their border”: in arrogance and pride they raided the borders of Judah (Jer 48:29; 49:1).

Therefore as I live, saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, Surely Moab shall be as Sodom, and the children of Ammon as Gomorrah, even the breeding of nettles, and saltpits, and a perpetual desolation.

entries.section: 3. The judgment of Moab and Ammon:

paragraphs.text: The residue of my people shall spoil them, and the remnant of my people shall possess them. [9]

The fate of the Moabites and the Ammonites becomes like the fate of Sodom and Gomorrah, where every remembrance of them comes to an end, and their lands are turned into a desolation without inhabitant. Their land produces nettles, a plant with thorny hairs, instead of wheat, and their springs produce exceedingly salty waters instead of springs of sweet water, and they become spoil for Israel.

entries.section: 3. The judgment of Moab and Ammon:

paragraphs.text: This shall they have for their pride, because they have reproached and magnified themselves against the people of the LORD of hosts. [10]
What comes upon them is not arbitrary; rather it is the natural fruit of their pride and their arrogance against the people of the LORD of hosts.

entries.section: 3. The judgment of Moab and Ammon:

paragraphs.text: The LORD will be terrible unto them: for he will famish all the gods of the earth; and men shall worship him, every one from his place, even all the isles of the heathen. [11]

God affirms that there is no enmity in the heart of God toward any particular people or nation; rather the proud and blaspheming people fall under the yoke of their pride, blasphemy and evil. But God shatters the idols and raises up from all the nations a people for Himself, in which every nation worships Him, indeed every man in his place. There is no need for all to go up to Jerusalem and worship in the temple of Solomon.
This is what God was preparing His ancient people to accept, namely that the earth and the fullness thereof become the Lord’s and His Christ’s.
“Sing unto God, ye kingdoms of the earth; O sing praises unto the Lord; Selah” (Ps 68:32).
“And the LORD shall be known to Egypt, and the Egyptians shall know the LORD in that day, and shall do sacrifice and oblation; yea, they shall vow a vow unto the LORD, and perform it” (Isa 19:21).

“For from the rising of the sun even unto the going down of the same my name shall be great among the Gentiles; and in every place incense shall be offered unto my name, and a pure offering…” (Mal 1:11).

He lowers the standing of the pagan gods, so that they become exceedingly lean, like predatory beasts that have grown very lean for lack of food for a long time. No sacrifice is offered to them any more, nor is any worship offered in their temples.

* Let us now hear another prophet who presents the same prophecy, saying that the worship of God will no longer be limited to one place, but the time will come when every man will know Him. He is Zephaniah, who says: “The Lord will appear to all the nations, and will famish all the gods of the nations; then every one will worship Him from his place” (Zeph 2:11) LXX. However, this was forbidden to the Jews, since Moses commanded them to worship in one place.

* You hear that the prophets declared beforehand, prophesying that men will no longer be limited to a place, coming from all the earth to offer sacrifice in one city (or one place), but each one will remain in his house (his homeland) and serve God and honor Him. What time is like the present time in which it has been possible for these prophecies to be fulfilled? In any case, listen and understand how the Gospels and the Apostle Paul agree with Zephaniah. The prophet said: “The Lord will appear,” and Paul said: “For the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all the people” (Titus 2:11). Zephaniah said: “to all the nations,” and Paul said: “to all men” (Titus 2:11). Zephaniah said: “He will famish your gods,” and Paul said: “Teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world” (Titus 2:12).

St. John Chrysostom * You do not believe that it was foretold to us that these nations would come to a place of God, as it was said: “Unto thee shall the Gentiles come from the ends of the earth” (Jer 16:19). Understand, if you can, that the peoples of these nations come to the God of the Christians, who is the true Most High God, not by walking but by faith. For this very declaration was presented in these words by another prophet: “The LORD will be terrible unto them: for he will famish all the gods of the earth; and men shall worship him, every one from his place, even all the isles of the heathen” (Zeph 2:11). One prophet says: “Unto thee shall the Gentiles come from the ends of the earth,” and the other says: “Every one shall worship him from his place.” Therefore they are not required to withdraw from their places in order to come to Him, since they find Him, whom they believe, in their hearts.
* They will come to Him without leaving their places, for by faith in Him they find Him in their hearts.

* For a long time… the demons kept silence in their temples concerning the things that were to happen, although it was not possible for them to be without knowledge of them, because of the utterances of the prophets. But recently, as the events began to draw near, the demons wished to announce them beforehand, so that they might not appear ignorant or defeated. Yet they did not point to certain things that had been announced beforehand and recorded long ago, such as those found in the prophet Zephaniah: “The Lord will overcome them and drive out all the gods of the nations from the earth. And every man will worship Him from his place, all the isles of the nations” (Zeph 2:11). Perhaps those gods who were worshipped in the temples of the nations did not believe that these events would be fulfilled with regard to them, and therefore did not wish to cause irritation among the seers and diviners, the soothsayers who followed them.

St. Augustine * Let us speak also of the churches as islands. Add to this that Scripture says in another place: “Many islands have returned to me” (Isa 42:10) LXX. The prophet Isaiah says in the name of the Lord: “Speak to the inhabitants of this island,” “Let many islands rejoice.” Just as islands stand in the midst of the sea, so churches are established in the midst of the world, and are beaten and struck by many waves of persecutions. Truly these islands are tossed by the waves every day, but they are not overwhelmed by the waters. Surely they are in the midst of the sea, but their foundation is Christ, Christ who cannot be shaken.

St. Jerome * Despite all this, they were still unable to rebuild the temple and restore the place in which they were permitted to practice their rites according to the Law. For the authority of Christ, the authority that founded the Church, destroyed that place. The prophet had foretold that Christ would come, though He would not come except after the captivity.
St. John Chrysostom

entries.section: 4. The judgment of Cush:

paragraphs.text: Ye Ethiopians also.
Ye shall be slain by my sword. [12]
Nebuchadnezzar subdued Cush (Jer 46:9-10; Ezek 30:4). The Lord says: “my sword,” and means by it Nebuchadnezzar, whom God used as an instrument in His hand for disciplining the nations.

entries.section: 5. The judgment of Assyria:

paragraphs.text: 13 And he will stretch out his hand against the north, and destroy Assyria; and will make Nineveh a desolation, and dry like a wilderness. 14 And flocks shall lie down in the midst of her, all the beasts of the nations: both the cormorant and the bittern shall lodge in the upper lintels of it; a voice shall croak in the windows; desolation shall be in the thresholds: for her cedar work is laid bare. 15 This is the rejoicing city that dwelt carelessly, that said in her heart, I am, and there is none beside me: how is she become a desolation, a place for beasts to lie down in! every one that passeth by her shall hiss, and wag his hand.
And he will stretch out his hand against the north, and destroy Assyria; and will make Nineveh a desolation, and dry like a wilderness. [13]
The Lord destroyed the Assyrian Empire and made its capital, “Nineveh,” a desolation.
And flocks shall lie down in the midst of her, all the beasts of the nations.
Both the cormorant and the bittern shall lodge in the upper lintels of it.
A voice shall croak in the windows.
Desolation shall be in the thresholds.

entries.section: 5. The judgment of Assyria:

paragraphs.text: For her cedar work is laid bare. [14]

Assyria is transformed from a great empire feared by all the nations of the world into wide wildernesses in which are found all kinds of animals, that is, domestic animals such as sheep, and predatory beasts. They become pastures without a law to govern them and without walls to protect the flocks. Its constitution becomes predation and death! As for birds, there is none in it except those that the Easterners considered gloomy birds, whose voices bring depression, sorrow and gloom, like the cormorant. Its birds do not know joyful songs but wailing in the windows.

When ruin and destruction come, the windows of the palaces stand open, and the birds perch on them mourning and lamenting. By the forces of nature the ceilings of the palaces, made of cedar wood as splendid works of art, are exposed, and these pieces lose their beauty and become a shelter for birds and insects. They become bare as the garment of their radiant beauty is stripped from them.

If Nineveh, the symbol of the wicked heart that is determined not to return to the Lord, has become a dwelling for the cormorant, which never ceases wailing and crying out, then the spiritual Jerusalem, the symbol of the holy heart, is a dwelling for the turtledove that rejoices continually. “The voice of the turtledove is heard in our land” (Song 2:12). It is as though the lot of the wicked is gloom full of despair, while the lot of the righteous is exultation full of hope. The heart of the wicked bears the earnest of hell, and the heart of the righteous bears the earnest of the eternal, heavenly, joyful Kingdom.

Assyria, which took Israel captive, was known for its extreme violence in dealing with captives. The kings found their delight in cutting off some members of the captives’ bodies, especially the rich and the nobles, and parading them in a mocking procession before the people; therefore it signifies the wicked, violent man, defiled with abominations. This state is turned into a lair of animals and none dwells in it except the cormorant and the hedgehog, and it becomes a desolation. But the holy soul becomes a joyful paradise full of the trees of virtue, and in it is heard the voice of the doves.
The following are the comments of St. Gregory, bishop of Nyssa, on what is said in the Song of Songs (Song 2:12).

* The echo of the voice makes the season delightful, and the singing of the birds resounds in the orchards, and the sweet echo of the turtledove’s voice reaches our ears… He has come who gave spring to our souls. He commanded the wind of evil that had stirred up the sea to be still: “And he said unto the sea, Peace, be still. And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm” (Mk 4:39). So everything became calm and our life began to flourish and was adorned with buds and flowers, and the flowers represent the virtue in our life that bears fruit in its seasons. Therefore the Word of God says: “For, lo, the winter is past, the rain is over and gone; the flowers appear on the earth; the time of pruning is come, and the voice of the turtledove is heard in our land” (Song 2:11-12)…

The Bridegroom says: “Behold, the meadows are flourishing with the flowers of virtue. Do you see this purity in the beauty of the fragrant narcissus? Do you see the rose of humility and the violet, which represents the sweet fragrance of the Lord Christ? Why, then, do you not make a crown of these flowers? For this is the season for cutting the flowers! And you make a branch into a crown to adorn yourself? The season of pruning has come. The voice of the turtledove bears witness to this; it resembles ‘the voice of one crying in the wilderness’ (Mt 3:3), for John the Baptist is the turtledove. He is the one who went before this luminous spring, who brought forth for the sons of men the wonderful flowers for cutting, and offered them to everyone who desired to gather them. It is he who showed us ‘there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse’ (Isa 11:1), and he is ‘the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world’ (Jn 1:29). And it is he who showed us repentance from sin and life according to virtue. The text says: ‘The voice of the turtledove is heard in our land’: and it calls ‘O land’ of those who were condemned for their sin, those whom the Gospel calls the tax collectors and the harlots, who heard the voice of John the Baptist while the rest did not accept his teaching.”
St. Gregory of Nyssa This is the rejoicing city that dwelt carelessly, that said in her heart:
I am, and there is none beside me.
How is she become a desolation, a place for beasts to lie down in!

entries.section: 5. The judgment of Assyria:

paragraphs.text: Every one that passeth by her shall hiss, and wag his hand. [15]

Nineveh was a rejoicing city that many longed to behold; its circumference was 60 miles, and the height of its walls about 100 feet, and three chariots side by side could drive upon its walls, and 1,500 watchtowers rose upon the walls. It became a desolation, so that it became difficult for anyone to know its location.

In arrogance Nineveh, like Babylon afterward and other arrogant lands, thought that it was the mistress of the world. The Lord says in Isaiah: “Therefore hear now this, thou that art given to pleasures, that dwellest carelessly, that sayest in thine heart, I am, and none else beside me; I shall not sit as a widow, neither shall I know the loss of children: But these two things shall come to thee in a moment in one day, the loss of children, and widowhood” (Isa 47:8-9).

The city of Nineveh represents the soul that is self-reliant and self-sufficient, not in God, and so it amuses itself in the world and thinks that it is in peace and security, and that no one can stand before it.
May You shatter my evil, and establish Your righteousness in me!
* Let my soul gather together with the souls of all Your people.
Let us gather together by Your Holy Spirit.
Expose before my eyes my audacity and my arrogance.
Burn up all evil within me and in my conduct, and grant me Your righteousness as a covering for my depths.
* Sin has made me like chaff in the blast of the winds.
I cannot stand before Your wrath.
Who is justified before You, O Holy One?
Your fiery Spirit renews my nature and turns me from chaff into holy wheat!
* To You I flee, O Savior; You take away my misery and grant me Your mercy.
In place of my arrogance, You grant me Your gentleness and Your humility.
You are my fortress; in You I hide, and You cover my weakness.
* Remove from within me every trace of idolatry.
Shatter every image I have set up for myself in my foolishness.
And may You take possession of all my heart and my being.
Without You my soul becomes forsaken, abandoned and desolate.
Without You all life in me is rooted up.
Enter into my depths, and establish Your heavenly Kingdom.
So that I no longer become a wasteland, a pasture for sheep.
Let the voice of the turtledove be heard within me, singing and praising Your name.
And let there be no place within me for the cormorant and other crying birds.
Let no voice of wailing be heard, but exultation and joy.
* Reveal Yourself within me in the splendor of Your glory.
So that all pride and arrogance flee from within me.
I will not judge anyone, but I will judge myself.
And I will not gloat over those who are under discipline, for I am deserving of every punishment, even death!
* By Your passing into my depths You open my insight, and I see You, the Savior of the whole world.
I see all peoples and nations having rejected every idol, and gathered around You like a triumphant procession.
The unclean nations have become Your holy bride.
The peoples hostile to You have become the object of Your delight.
Your heavens rejoice and exult in the holy humanity in You.

entries.section: 1. The oppressing city:

paragraphs.text: 1 Woe to her that is filthy and polluted, to the oppressing city! 2 She obeyed not the voice; she received not correction; she trusted not in the LORD; she drew not near to her God. 3 Her princes within her are roaring lions; her judges are evening wolves; they gnaw not the bones till the morrow. 4 Her prophets are light and treacherous persons: her priests have polluted the sanctuary, they have done violence to the law. 5 The just LORD is in the midst thereof; he will not do iniquity: every morning doth he bring his judgment to light, he faileth not; but the unjust knoweth no shame. 6 “I have cut off the nations: their towers are desolate; I made their streets waste, that none passeth by: their cities are destroyed, so that there is no man, that there is none inhabitant. 7 I said, Surely thou wilt fear me, thou wilt receive instruction; so their dwelling should not be cut off, howsoever I punished them: but they rose early, and corrupted all their doings.
Woe to her that is rebellious, filthy and polluted, to the oppressing city! [1]

He describes Jerusalem with exceedingly shameful traits, calling her rebellious, unclean and oppressing. Outwardly she is the city of God, which ought to have been God’s agency, but by her conduct she is rebellious against Him, and so becomes worse than the pagan cities. She is the center of worship, for in her is the holy temple, but in her life she is unclean. This trait in Hebrew is Moreah, which is close to the word Mariah (Moriah), the name of the hill on which the temple was built. So instead of Moriah she became Moreah, that is, unclean, with no place in her for the holiness of God. And finally she is oppressing, bearing no witness to God’s mercies and His gentleness toward the classes that need help. In other words, He chose her as His city, but instead of obeying Him she became rebellious; in her He set up His temple for worship, but instead of holiness she became unclean; and He gave her the commandment of love and mercy toward the neighbor, but she became oppressing and does not listen to the divine commandment. The Lord commands the king of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, saying: “Execute ye judgment and righteousness, and deliver the spoiled out of the hand of the oppressor: and do no wrong, do no violence to the stranger, the fatherless, nor the widow, neither shed innocent blood in this place” (Jer 22:3).

Three grave traits make a people, like a person, lose fellowship with the holy God, the Giver of life, holiness and love. These traits are: rebellion or disobedience, uncleanness or lack of holiness, and finally oppression or injustice and lack of love. These three traits touch a person’s inner life, his relationship with God and his relationship with his brother. Rebellion is disobedience to God and failure to keep His commandment. Holiness touches most of all his inner depths. And oppression touches most of all his relationship with his brethren. Yet each trait has its repercussions on all three spheres, for there is no separation between obedience to God, a person’s sanctification and his love for his neighbor.

entries.section: A. Rebellion or disobedience:

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine, in explaining the psalmist’s words: “Through thy precepts I get understanding: therefore I hate every false way” (Ps 119:104), sees a link between these three traits. For he sees in obedience to God’s commandments the enjoyment of the wealth of the knowledge of wisdom, and by this wealth a person loathes every way of evil, loves righteousness and hates injustice.

* By obedience to God’s commandments (the psalmist) attains the understanding of the things he longs to know… These are the words of the spiritual members of Christ: “Through thy precepts I get understanding”… For those who keep the commandments receive greater riches in the knowledge of wisdom… and by love of righteousness he hates all injustice… The heavenly wisdom is given to him who obeys God and receives understanding from His commandments.
St. Augustine * Nothing pleases God like obedience.
St. Jerome

entries.section: B. As for holiness, it was said:

paragraphs.text: * O God, Thy way is in holiness: “Thy way, O God, is in the sanctuary” (Ps 77:13). If you are not holy, the way of God is not in you. What is the way of God? “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (Jn 14:6). It is the Savior who says this. Therefore the way is the Son of God. The way of God is the holy man alone. If we want Christ to dwell in us, let us be holy, for the way of God is holiness.

* The man of holiness need not fear that fire: “A fire goeth before him, and burneth up his enemies round about” (Ps 97:3); let the sinner fear it. For the fire purifies the saints and burns the sinners: “A fire goeth before him.” “Who maketh his angels spirits; his ministers a flaming fire” (Ps 104:4).
St. Jerome

entries.section: C. Concerning injustice it was said:

paragraphs.text: * Just as there can be no agreement between Christ and Belial, and between righteousness and unrighteousness (2 Cor 6:14-15), so it is impossible for one soul to love both goodness and evil. You who love the Lord, that you may hate the evil one, Satan; in every work there is love for one and hatred for the other.

* The proud man possesses in his pride the source of all other evils, and offers no remorse, for he thinks that he is the object of God’s approval. Pride is against God, since it does not submit to Him, for the proud man reckons himself righteous. He does not repent of his evils, but rather boasts hypocritically of his good works.
St. Jerome She obeyed not the voice; she received not correction.

entries.section: C. Concerning injustice it was said:

paragraphs.text: She trusted not in the LORD; she drew not near to her God. [2]
Here He reveals Jerusalem’s incurable disease, which is her refusal of reform, her lack of trust in the heavenly Physician, and her flight from Him. Her disease bears three grave traits:
A. Her rejection of the voice of her heavenly Physician and her unwillingness to be reformed.
B. Her lack of trust in Him, as though He were unable to heal her and satisfy her needs.

C. Her failure to draw near to Him, as though she asked Him to depart from her and not dwell within her. The prophet Moses says: “For what nation is there so great, who hath God so nigh unto them, as the LORD our God is in all things that we call upon him for?” (Deut 4:7). He wishes to attribute Himself to her, so as to be called her God, but she withdraws and becomes a stranger to Him.

* She (Jerusalem) was so because she refused to the end to listen to the word of the prophet sent to her, and did not by any means accept teaching from the source. And although she seemed to promise change for a time, she returned again to her evil traits. In any case she did not care that God had sent the prophet to her, and did not decide to listen to him in the end, despising such a wonderful experience. On the contrary, she forgot Him completely and declared war against Him, attacking Jerusalem after the destruction of the ten tribes, the city in which the temple of God was found.

Theodore of Mopsuestia It is remarkable that the heavenly Physician came down to us and drew near to us, yet we refuse to draw near to Him. Therefore it is fitting for us to cry out with the psalmist, saying: “Unto thee, O LORD, do I lift up my soul. O my God, I trust in thee” (Ps 25:1-2).

* “Unto thee, O LORD, do I lift up my soul”; by spiritual longing I lift up my soul that has been brought low to the earth by carnal desires. “O my God, I trust in thee: let me not be ashamed” (Ps 25:2). My God, by relying on myself I came to this weakness of the flesh. I who, by forsaking God, longed to be like God, fear death from the smallest insects. Now, in mockery, I am put to shame by my pride: “I trust in thee: let me not be ashamed.”

St. Augustine * “Blessed is the man whom thou chastenest, O LORD” (Ps 94:12). Blessed is the man who accepts God as his teacher… Blessed is the man whom You train, O Lord, and teach in Your law, in Your holy books… for they give him rest in the days of adversity, until the pit is dug for the sinner (the wicked).
St. Jerome The prophet presents to us a wonderful concept of religiousness, namely drawing near to God, for He wants us to cleave to Him.

* “The LORD reigneth, he is clothed with majesty” (Ps 93:1). The Lord is King; He has put on the majesty of the Fathers (the patriarchs), the prophets and the believing people. He puts on majesty; as though the patriarchs (Abraham, Isaac and Jacob) and the prophets were the garment of Christ. They are the girdle that is referred to in Jeremiah. Do you want to know that the saints are like the girdle of God and His garment? God Himself says: [For as the girdle cleaveth to the loins of a man, so have I made myself cleave to my people] (cf. Jer 13:11). The people of God cleave to Him, as a man’s garment clings to his body. But because this girdle, or this glory with which the Lord is clothed, was cast to the other side of the Euphrates and thrown into a cleft of the rock, it was spoiled (Jer 13:4-12)… The Lord is not naked, for He cannot remain without a girdle; He cannot be without a covering. So when He lost the first people, He made for Himself a garment from the nations.
St. Jerome Her princes within her are roaring lions.

entries.section: C. Concerning injustice it was said:

paragraphs.text: Her judges are evening wolves; they gnaw not the bones till the morrow. [3]

Her leaders were grave examples of evil, injustice and predation; these ought to have been physicians for her, treating her diseases, but behold, they are like roaring lions in her midst and like evening wolves that prey by night and leave no trace of the prey in the morning. They ravage all who are around them, careless of the Mosaic Law or the natural law.

As for the judges, in their flattery of the princes who are like lions, they walk in darkness like wolves that appear in the evening to prey and devour. They eat flesh and bone so that they leave nothing of the prey till the morning.

entries.section: C. Concerning injustice it was said:

paragraphs.text: Her prophets are light and treacherous persons: her priests have polluted the sanctuary, they have done violence to the law. [4]
